paras: The reported lynching of James Massey refers to the disappearance in May 1888 of a Cheatham County, Tennessee, man arrested on a charge of attempted rape, whom citizens were believed to have lynched while he was being taken to Ashland City. Dispatches from Clarksville first called a lynching probable and then said he had probably been lynched, but no report confirming his death appears in the coverage.

Massey, who lived in Cheatham County, was charged with attempting to rape Miss Weakley, whom the dispatches described as "a prominent young lady" and "a respectable young lady" of the county. According to the Clarksville dispatch, Miss Weakley was afterward "completely prostrated" and ill.

On May 24, 1888, Massey was arrested near Clarksville and taken to Ashland City, the Cheatham County seat, which the dispatch called "the scene of his crime." The same report said the citizens were "greatly enraged" and that a lynching was probable. A day later, a Clarksville special to the Nashville American stated that nothing had been heard of Massey since he left Clarksville for Ashland City and that "it is believed indignant citizens have lynched him."
No follow-up report of a body, an inquest, a release or a trial was found, and the outcome is not established by the coverage.

The story reached the white press only as brief telegraphic items from Clarksville, carried far from Tennessee. The Rock Island Daily Argus in Illinois ran the May 25 dispatch under the headline "Probably Been Lynched," and the Press and Daily Dakotaian at Yankton printed it the next day as "Probably Lynched." The Hickman Courier in Kentucky printed the earlier May 24 dispatch, headed "Lynching Probable," in its June 1 news column, after the later report had already circulated.
None of the items gave Massey's race; they described the accuser's standing, called Ashland City "the scene of his crime," and reported the expected lynching without comment.

reader.title: Reported lynching of James Massey
bases: A Clarksville dispatch reported a lynching 'probable' after Massey's arrest on a charge of attempted rape (A3), and a second said it was 'believed' citizens had lynched him (A1); no killing is confirmed.

The only report of a killing is a belief that 'indignant citizens' had lynched Massey after he dropped from sight (A1); no body, inquest or eyewitness account appears, and the earlier dispatch reports only a threat (A3). The pretext was an accusation of attempted rape (A1, A3).
Both dispatches came from Clarksville a day apart (A3, A1), A2 reprints A1, and the claimed lynching rests on one dispatch that states only a belief.
